1G (Linear Algebra)

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 106
1G OurBigBook.com
The dual map reverses the direction of the linear map:
α∗:W∗⟶V∗,α∗(λ)=λ∘α.​
(1)
Here the dual spaces consist of complex-linear functionals. Composition with α is linear both as a functional on V and as an operation on W∗, so this does define a linear map between the dual spaces.
Let (v1​,…,vn​) and (w1​,…,wm​) be the chosen bases, and let (v1,…,vn) and (w1,…,wm) be their dual bases. If A represents α, then α(vi​)=∑j​Aji​wj​. Therefore
(α∗wj)(vi​)=wj(α(vi​))=Aji​,α∗wj=∑i​Aji​vi.
(2)
The coefficient in row i, column j of the matrix of α∗ is thus Aji​, giving the matrix transpose AT. This calculation introduces no complex conjugation: the algebraic dual map uses complex-linear functionals, whereas a Hermitian transpose belongs to the inner-product adjoint construction.

2G (Groups, Rings and Modules)

Words: 72 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 72
2G OurBigBook.com
The Fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups expresses every finite abelian group of this order as a product of cyclic groups of prime-power order. Their exponents correspond to the partitions of an integer 4:
Cp4​,Cp3​×Cp​,Cp2​×Cp2​,Cp2​×Cp​×Cp​,Cp4​.​
(3)
These are pairwise nonisomorphic: the largest order of a group element distinguishes all except the two groups with largest element order p2, and those have respectively p2 and p3 elements annihilated by multiplication by p. The classification exhausts the possibilities, so there are five isomorphism classes.

∀ε>0 ∃N ∀n≥N ∀x∈(0,1):∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣<ε.​

For each fixed x>0, continuity of the logarithm gives the pointwise convergence fn​(x)→logx. But at xn​=1/n, which belongs to (0,1) for n>1,
fn​(xn​)−logxn​=log1/n2/n​=log2.
(5)
Consequently the uniform error cannot tend to zero. In fact fn​(x)−logx=log(1+1/(nx)) is unbounded as x↓0 for every fixed n. The pointwise limit is logx, and convergence is not uniform.

Words: 199 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 199
4H OurBigBook.com
The argument principle states that if h is meromorphic on a neighbourhood of a positively oriented simple closed contour and its interior, with neither zeros nor poles on the contour, then
2πi1​∮γ​h(z)h′(z)​dz=N−P,
(7)
where N and P count its interior zeros and poles with multiplicity. This integer is also the winding number of h(γ) about zero.
Fix z0​∈U. Injectivity prevents f from being constant on a neighbourhood of z0​, so its Taylor expansion has the form
f(z)−f(z0​)=(z−z0​)mh(z),m≥1,h(z0​)=0.
(8)
Choose a small closed disk D⊂U, centred at z0​, such that h and mh+(z−z0​)h′ are nonzero throughout D. Then f−f(z0​) has its sole zero at z0​ in D, of multiplicity m, while f′ has no zero in D∖{z0​}. On its boundary let δ=min∣f−f(z0​)∣>0.
Choose 0<∣w∣<δ. For every 0≤t≤1, the holomorphic function f−f(z0​)−tw is nonzero on ∂D. By the argument principle, its number of zeros is an integer given by a contour integral varying continuously with t, hence remains m. At t=1 none of these zeros is z0​, so their derivatives are nonzero and they are simple zeros. Thus there are m distinct points taking the value f(z0​)+w. Injectivity forces m=1, proving f′(z0​)=0 everywhere in U.

5B (Methods)

Words: 148 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 148
5B OurBigBook.com
Take the wave speed c>0 and introduce characteristic coordinates ξ=x+ct, η=x−ct. The chain rule gives
∂x​=∂ξ​+∂η​,∂t​=c∂ξ​−c∂η​,ytt​−c2yxx​=−4c2yξη​.
(9)
The wave equation therefore says yξη​=0. Integrating first with respect to η gives yξ​=F(ξ), and integrating with respect to ξ gives y=f(x+ct)+g(x−ct) with twice differentiable f,g. Conversely substitution shows that every such sum solves the wave equation. The two terms are travelling waves of unchanged shape, moving respectively to the left and right at speed c.
The zero initial displacement gives g(x)=−f(x), and the initial velocity gives 2cf′(x)=ψ(x). Hence the D'Alembert formula with initial velocity is
y(x,t)=2c1​∫x−ctx+ct​ψ(s)ds.​
(10)
For a classical twice differentiable solution one may take ψ∈C1. Differentiation gives yt​(x,0)=ψ(x) and y(x,0)=0 directly. The coordinate calculation also works for any nonzero signed c, with physical speed ∣c∣. If the printed constant is allowed to be c=0, the equation instead gives y=A(x)+tB(x) and these initial data give y=tψ(x); the displayed travelling-wave representation requires c=0.

For the wavefunction of a particle of mass m, the probability density and probability current are
ρ=Ψ∗Ψ,j=2miℏ​(Ψ∗Ψx​−ΨΨx∗​)=mℏ​Im(Ψ∗Ψx​).​
(11)
For a real potential V, the Time-dependent Schrödinger equation and its complex conjugate read
iℏΨt​=−2mℏ2​Ψxx​+VΨ,−iℏΨt∗​=−2mℏ2​Ψxx∗​+VΨ∗.
(12)
Multiplying by Ψ∗ and Ψ respectively yields
ρt​=2miℏ​(Ψ∗Ψxx​−ΨΨxx∗​)=−jx​.
(13)
The potential terms cancel because V is real. This is the continuity equation, expressing local conservation of probability.
For the given superposition the common time phase cancels in Ψ∗Ψx​, and
Ψ∗Ψx​=ik(1−∣R∣2)+ik(R∗e2ikx−Re−2ikx).
(14)
The expression in the second parentheses is purely imaginary, so the second term is real and contributes nothing to the probability current. Thus
j=mℏk​(1−∣R∣2).​
(15)
It is the incoming probability current minus the reflected probability current.

7E (Electromagnetism)

Words: 171 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 171
7E OurBigBook.com
For a moving circuit, Faraday's law takes the form
E(t)=∮C(t)​(E+v×B)⋅dℓ=−dtd​∫S(t)​B⋅ndS.​
(16)
Here C(t) is the instantaneous wire contour, v its local material velocity, and S(t) any spanning surface. The contour orientation and surface normal vector obey the right-hand convention. The integral on the right is the magnetic flux, differentiated with both the field and circuit position allowed to vary. The electric field term is the electric force per unit electric charge around the wire, and v×B supplies the motional electromotive force. Their sum is the electromotive force driving charge around the moving circuit. The condition ∇⋅B=0 makes the magnetic flux independent of the spanning surface.
Choose the initial loop normal vector to be +ey​, so rotation about +ez​ gives n(t)=(−sinΩt,cosΩt,0). The spatially uniform magnetic field gives
Φ(t)=πa2B0​[−sinΩtcosωt+cosΩtsinωt]=πa2B0​sin((ω−Ω)t).
(17)
Using Ohm's law for the resistive loop,
I(t)=Rπa2B0​(Ω−ω)​cos((ω−Ω)t).​
(18)
Positive electric current is measured in the contour orientation associated with n(t). Reversing that convention reverses the signed answer. When Ω=ω, the magnetic flux is constant and the induced electric current vanishes. This uses the usual thin resistive-circuit approximation with self-inductance neglected.

L(f)=∫02​K(t)f(3)(t)dt,K(t)=L(2(x−t)+2​​).
(19)
This representation also follows by applying L to the Taylor expansion of f with integral remainder. The derivative at zero of the truncated quadratic is zero for t≥0, and its sampled values give
K(t)=−(1−t)+2​+41​(2−t)2={t−43​t2,41​(2−t)2,​0≤t≤1,1≤t≤2.​
(20)
The Peano kernel is nonnegative, and
∫02​∣K(t)∣dt=[2t2​−4t3​]01​+∫12​4(2−t)2​dt=41​+121​=31​.
(21)
Hence ∣L(f)∣≤31​∥f(3)∥∞​. For f(x)=x3/6, the third derivative is 1, while f′(0)=0 and μ(f)=−1/3. Thus equality holds, proving the least constant is c=1/3, attained by f(x)=x3/6.

i OurBigBook.com
For a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition matrix P, two states are communicating states when each can be reached from the other with positive probability in finitely many steps:
i↔j⟺∃m,n≥0: (Pm)ij​>0, (Pn)ji​>0.​
(22)
The convention P0=I includes communication of a state with itself.

ii

Words: 38 Articles: 1
9C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 38
ii OurBigBook.com
Let Ti+​=inf{n≥1:Xn​=i} be the first positive return time. A recurrent state is one for which
Pi​(Ti+​<∞)=1.​
(23)
The subscript means that the Markov chain starts at i. The positive-time condition distinguishes a genuine return from the automatic visit at time zero.

Solution

Words: 172
9C OurBigBook.com
Communication is reflexive because (P0)ii​=1, and symmetric by its definition. If i↔j and j↔k, choose positive-probability paths i→j in m steps and j→k in n steps. The Chapman-Kolmogorov equation gives
(Pm+n)ik​≥(Pm)ij​(Pn)jk​>0.
(24)
Combining the reverse paths gives a positive-probability path k→i as well. Thus communication is transitive and is an equivalence relation.
To transfer recurrence, first establish the recurrence criterion by return probabilities. Put ri​=Pi​(Ti+​<∞) and let Ni​=∑n≥0​1{Xn​=i}​ under Pi​. After each return the Strong Markov property restarts the chain at i, so Pi​(Ni​≥k+1)=rik​. Therefore
∑n≥0​(Pn)ii​=Ei​Ni​=∑k≥0​rik​.
(25)
For ri​<1 this equals (1−ri​)−1; for ri​=1 it is infinite. The expectation identity follows by summing the nonnegative indicators, so remains valid when the expectation is infinite. Consequently i is a recurrent state exactly when its return-probability series diverges.
If i↔j, choose a,b with (Pa)ji​>0 and (Pb)ij​>0. For every n≥0,
(Pa+n+b)jj​≥(Pa)ji​(Pn)ii​(Pb)ij​.
(26)
Summing over n, recurrence of i forces the return-probability series for j to diverge. The proved criterion shows j is recurrent, so recurrence is a property of the communicating class.

The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square complex matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: if χA​(t)=det(tI−A)=tn+cn−1​tn−1+⋯+c0​, then
An+cn−1​An−1+⋯+c0​I=0.​
(27)
For a proof, expand the adjugate matrix as adj(tI−A)=∑k=0n−1​Bk​tk. The adjugate identity gives
(tI−A)∑k=0n−1​Bk​tk=χA​(t)I.
(28)
Comparing coefficients yields −AB0​=c0​I, Bk−1​−ABk​=ck​I for 1≤k≤n−1, and Bn−1​=I. Multiply the middle identities on the left by Ak, include the first identity, and add AnBn−1​=An. The terms involving the Bk​ cancel consecutively:
−AB0​+∑k=1n−1​(AkBk−1​−Ak+1Bk​)+AnBn−1​=0.
(29)
Their right sides sum to c0​I+∑k=1n−1​ck​Ak+An. This proves the theorem without any substitution of noncommuting matrices into a scalar polynomial identity.

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
For a 2×2 matrix, the characteristic polynomial is t2−tr(A)t+detA. The given matrix trace and determinant therefore make it t2+1. By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, A2=−I, and hence A4=I. Since A2=I, the order of a group element A cannot be 1 or 2. If A3=I, then A=A4(A3)−1=I, also impossible. Thus the order is 4.

Solution

Words: 231
i OurBigBook.com
First, the orbit-stabilizer theorem applied to a face gives ∣G∣=20⋅3=60: its stabilizer subgroup consists of the identity and the two rotations through 120∘ about the axis through the centres of that face and its opposite. A rotation preserving a face must preserve its outward normal and cyclically permute its three vertices, so there are no further stabilizing rotations.
The conjugacy classes are as follows:
  • The identity: size 1.
  • Half-turns about axes through midpoints of opposite edges: size 15.
  • Rotations through ±2π/3 about opposite-face axes: size 20.
  • Rotations through ±2π/5 about opposite-vertex axes: size 12.
  • Rotations through ±4π/5 about opposite-vertex axes: size 12.
There are 30/2=15 edge axes, 20/2=10 face axes, and 12/2=6 vertex axes. They give respectively 15, 2⋅10=20, and 4⋅6=24 distinct nonidentity rotations, already accounting for all 59 nonidentity elements.
To justify the class assertions, conjugation by a rotation carries the rotation axis to its image and preserves the rotation angle about the transported oriented axis. The transitive group action on edges puts all half-turns in one conjugacy class. The transitive group action on faces puts the 120∘ rotations defined using outward face normals in one conjugacy class; opposite faces encode opposite signs about the same unoriented axis. The same reasoning with outward vertex directions gives a class of twelve 72∘ rotations and a class of twelve 144∘ rotations, including their inverses. These last classes cannot merge: the matrix trace of a three-dimensional rotation is 1+2cosθ, which differs for θ=2π/5 and 4π/5. Thus the list is complete.

ii

Words: 68 Articles: 1
11G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 68
ii OurBigBook.com
The face action gives ∣G∣=60, as calculated above. Every normal subgroup contains the identity and is a union of whole conjugacy classes. Thus its possible order is 1 plus a subset sum of 15,20,12,12. The distinct resulting numbers are
1,13,16,21,25,28,33,36,40,45,48,60.
(30)
By Lagrange's theorem for finite groups, a subgroup order divides 60. Only 1 and 60 in this list do so. Consequently the normal subgroups are {1} and G, and the rotational symmetry group of a regular icosahedron is a simple group.

12A (Geometry)

Words: 244 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 244
12A OurBigBook.com
In the Poincaré half-plane model, H={x+iy:y>0} has Riemannian metric
ds2=y2dx2+dy2​.​
(31)
Its orientation-preserving isometries are the Möbius transformations z↦(az+b)/(cz+d) with real coefficients and ad−bc=1, with a simultaneous sign change representing the same map. The full isometry group also contains their compositions with z↦−z, which reverse orientation. The hyperbolic lines are vertical Euclidean lines and upper semicircles centred on the real axis; each meets the boundary orthogonally.
A hyperbolic line with finite endpoints p<q is mapped to the imaginary axis by
T(z)=q−zz−p​.
(32)
Its coefficient determinant is q−p>0, so rescaling the coefficients makes this an orientation-preserving isometry. The endpoints map to 0 and ∞, which characterize the imaginary-axis hyperbolic line. For a vertical line with endpoints p,∞, use T(z)=z−p. If T1​,T2​ send the two prescribed lines to the imaginary axis, T2−1​T1​ sends the first to the second. This proves transitivity on hyperbolic lines.
For two ultraparallel hyperbolic lines, choose their common perpendicular and map it to the imaginary axis. A hyperbolic line perpendicular to that axis is a semicircle centred at zero: orthogonality at iy forces the circle centre to have real coordinate zero. Thus the reflecting lines become semicircles of distinct radii r1​,r2​>0. The hyperbolic reflection in the radius-r semicircle is Sr​(z)=r2/z; it fixes that semicircle pointwise and reverses orientation. Their composition is
Sr2​​Sr1​​(z)=λz,λ=(r2​/r1​)2=1.
(33)
Its kth power is z↦λkz, and no positive power is the identity since λ>0 and λ=1. Conjugation by the chosen isometry preserves order of a group element, so the original composition has infinite order. Reversing the order of the reflections replaces λ by λ−1 and gives the same conclusion.

The contraction mapping theorem says that if (X,d) is a nonempty complete metric space and T:X→X satisfies d(Tx,Ty)≤qd(x,y) for a constant 0≤q<1, then T has exactly one fixed point.
For the proof, start at x0​∈X and set xn​=Tnx0​. Iterating the contraction bound gives d(xn+1​,xn​)≤qnd(x1​,x0​). The triangle inequality then gives, for m>n,
d(xm​,xn​)≤∑k=nm−1​qkd(x1​,x0​)≤1−qqn​d(x1​,x0​).
(34)
Thus (xn​) is a Cauchy sequence and has a limit x∗​ by completeness. Since the contraction is continuous, Tx∗​=limTxn​=limxn+1​=x∗​. If y∗​ is another fixed point, then d(x∗​,y∗​)≤qd(x∗​,y∗​), forcing distance zero. This proves existence and uniqueness.
For the integral map, the fundamental theorem of calculus shows that Tf is continuous whenever f is continuous. In the supremum norm,
∣Tf(x)−Tg(x)∣≤3∥f−g∥∞​​∫0x​∣t∣dt​=23​x2∥f−g∥∞​.
(35)
Hence ∥Tf−Tg∥∞​≤23​max(a2,b2)∥f−g∥∞​. We can choose
a=−21​,b=21​,q=83​.​
(36)
The space C[a,b] with this supremum norm is complete: a uniformly Cauchy sequence has pointwise real limits, the Cauchy bound passes to those limits to give uniform convergence, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. The contraction mapping theorem therefore gives a unique continuous y with y(x)=1+∫0x​3ty(t)dt. The fundamental theorem of calculus makes this y differentiable, with y′=3xy and y(0)=1. Conversely every solution of that initial-value problem obeys the integral equation, so uniqueness transfers to the ordinary differential equation. Explicitly y(x)=e3x2/2 on [−1/2,1/2], as direct differentiation confirms.

a OurBigBook.com
The closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed subsets containing A; equivalently it consists of the points whose every open neighbourhood meets A.
Suppose f is continuous and x∈cl(A). For any open neighbourhood V of f(x), continuity makes f−1(V) an open neighbourhood of x, so it meets A. Hence V meets f(A), showing f(x)∈cl(f(A)). This proves f(cl(A))⊆cl(f(A)).
Conversely suppose this inclusion holds for every subset A. For a closed subset C⊆Y, let A=f−1(C). Then f(A)⊆C and therefore cl(f(A))⊆C. By the assumed inclusion, f(cl(A))⊆C, so cl(A)⊆f−1(C)=A. Since A⊆cl(A) always, A is closed. Thus every closed set has closed preimage, equivalently every open set has open preimage. This is continuity, proving the claimed equivalence.

b

Words: 87 Articles: 1
14A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 87
b OurBigBook.com
For each integer n≥1, the open balls {B(x,1/n):x∈M} cover the compact metric space M. Compactness supplies a finite subcover with centres forming a finite set Sn​. Define S=⋃n≥1​Sn​, a countable union of finite sets and therefore countable.
For any x∈M and ε>0, choose n with 1/n<ε. One of the covering balls contains x, so there is s∈Sn​⊆S with d(x,s)<1/n<ε. Every open neighbourhood of x therefore meets S, giving x∈cl(S). Thus cl(S)=M, and S is a countable dense subset. If M is empty, simply take S=∅.

For fixed endpoints, the Euler-Lagrange equation is Fy​−dxd​Fy′​=0. Since F has no explicit dependence on x, differentiating gives
dxd​(F−y′Fy′​)=Fy​y′+Fy′​y′′−y′′Fy′​−y′dxd​Fy′​=y′(Fy​−dxd​Fy′​)=0.
(47)
Thus F−y′Fy′​=C, the Beltrami identity.
With r′=dr/dθ, the arc length element and the prescribed speed give the travel-time functional
T[r]=k1​∫0π/2​r2r′2+r2​​dθ.​
(48)
For the circular road r=a, this is Tcircle​=π/(2ka).
For the integrand F=r′2+r2​/r2, the Beltrami identity simplifies to
F−r′Fr′​=r′2+r2​1​=C.
(49)
The candidate r=a(cosθ+sinθ) has r′2+r2=2a2 and the required endpoints. To prove it really minimizes the travel time, rather than merely satisfies a first integral, put u=1/r. Then
r2r′2+r2​​=u′2+u2​.
(50)
This is the Euclidean arc length integrand for the inverted curve (X,Y)=(ucosθ,usinθ), whose endpoints are (1/a,0) and (0,1/a). Every connecting curve has length at least their Euclidean distance 2​/a, by the triangle inequality. Equality is attained by the straight line segment X+Y=1/a. In polar form it gives u(cosθ+sinθ)=1/a, hence the proposed r. It stays strictly positive throughout the interval. Consequently
r(θ)=a(cosθ+sinθ),Tmin​=ka2​​.​
(51)
This travel-time minimization with speed proportional to squared radius is globally solved by the inversion: its minimum is strictly less than π/(2ka).

mπ2​c4=(E1​+E2​)2−c2∣p1​+p2​∣2=2E1​E2​(1−cosθ)=4E1​E2​sin2(θ/2).

sin2θ​=2E1​E2​​mπ​c2​.​

In the pion rest frame, conservation of three-momentum makes the Electron and massless neutrino momenta equal and opposite, of common magnitude p. Their energies obey
Ee​+pc=mπ​c2,Ee2​=p2c2+me2​c4.
(54)
Squaring Ee​=mπ​c2−pc and cancelling p2c2 gives
pc=2mπ​mπ2​−me2​​c2,Ee​=2mπ​mπ2​+me2​​c2.

The Electron four-momentum satisfies p=Ee​v/c2. Thus, for the physically allowed decay mπ​>me​,
v=cmπ2​+me2​mπ2​−me2​​=c1+(me​/mπ​)21−(me​/mπ​)2​.​

18D (Fluid Dynamics)

Words: 350 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 350
18D OurBigBook.com
For constant mass density and incompressible flow, use (u⋅∇)u=∇(∣u∣2/2)−u×ω in the Euler equations for an inviscid fluid. Taking the curl removes the pressure and kinetic energy gradients, giving ωt​=∇×(u×ω). The supplied vector identity, with ∇⋅u=0 and ∇⋅ω=0, yields the vorticity equation
DtDω​=ωt​+(u⋅∇)ω=(ω⋅∇)u.​
(57)
In a two-dimensional flow u=(u,v,0) is independent of z, and ω=ωez​. The right side vanishes, so Dω/Dt=0: each material element retains its vorticity. The vortex lines are parallel to z and are carried by the planar velocity. Also planar incompressibility preserves the area of a material cross-section; integrating its conserved vorticity over that area shows that its circulation, or vortex strength, stays constant. Thus the vortex lines move with the fluid without changing strength.
Place a line vortex of circulation Γ at (0,b) above the wall y=0. Its velocity field is Γez​×(r−r0​)/(2π∣r−r0​∣2). The method of images puts a vortex of circulation −Γ at (0,−b). With u=(ψy​,−ψx​), the resulting stream function is
ψ(x,y)=−2πΓ​logx2+(y−b)2​+2πΓ​logx2+(y+b)2​.
(58)
It is identically zero on the wall, so uy​=−ψx​=0 there. In the fluid half-plane it has just the required vortex singularity, with no other singularities, and its velocity decays at infinity. This is the no-background-flow solution with the wall: the difference from another such solution is a regular irrotational, divergence-free decaying field with zero normal velocity. Reflect its tangential component evenly and its normal component oddly across the wall. The reflected components are bounded harmonic functions on the whole plane, so they are constant by harmonic Liouville theorem, and decay forces both constants to be zero. Thus replacing the wall by the image gives the same flow. The real vortex moves under the image velocity, excluding its own singular velocity, so
r˙0​=2π−Γ​4b2ez​×(0,2b)​=(4πbΓ​,0).
(59)
Its signed velocity parallel to the wall is Γ/(4πb), and its speed is ∣Γ∣/(4πb).
For the quarter-plane, place images of circulation −Γ at (−x,y) and (x,−y), and +Γ at (−x,−y). The paired stream functions make both walls streamlines. Summing their velocities at the real vortex gives
x˙=4πΓ​(y1​−x2+y2y​)=4πy(x2+y2)Γx2​,y˙​=4πΓ​(−x1​+x2+y2x​)=−4πx(x2+y2)Γy2​.
(60)
In polar coordinates,
r˙=rxx˙+yy˙​​=2πrΓ​cot2θ,θ˙=r2xy˙​−yx˙​=−4πr2Γ​.
(61)
It follows directly that
dtd​(rsin2θ)=r˙sin2θ+2rθ˙cos2θ=0.
(62)
Thus the line-vortex trajectory in a quarter-plane is rsin2θ=constant.

Write Sxx​=∑i​xi2​ and Yˉ=n−1∑i​Yi​. For an identifiable two-parameter linear regression assume Sxx​>0; for the variance estimate and test below also assume n>2. The least-squares normal equations are
∑i​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)=0,∑i​xi​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)=0.
(63)
Using ∑i​xi​=0 gives
α=Yˉ,β​=Sxx​∑i​xi​Yi​​.​
(64)
The residual sum of squares has positive-definite quadratic part nα2+Sxx​β2, so these equations give its unique minimum. The normal distribution of the independent errors gives the log-likelihood
ℓ(α,β,σ2)=−2n​log(2πσ2)−2σ21​∑i​(Yi​−α−βxi​)2.
(65)
For every fixed positive σ2, maximizing this over α,β is exactly minimizing the same residual sum of squares. Thus the ordinary least squares estimators are also the maximum-likelihood estimators.
The printed hypotheses do not explicitly require Sxx​>0 or n>2. If Sxx​=0, all xi​ vanish and β is unidentifiable; this is an intercept-only model with n−1 residual degrees of freedom. For n=1 its residual is identically zero, so the likelihood has no finite maximizer with positive variance. If Sxx​>0 but n=2, the fit is saturated, leaving no residual variance estimate or Student test with positive degrees of freedom. The following nondegenerate formulas use Sxx​>0 and n>2.

Let RSS=∑i​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)2. Differentiating the log-likelihood in v=σ2 gives
∂v∂ℓ​=−2vn​+2v2RSS​.
(66)
For RSS>0 this changes from positive to negative at v=RSS/n, so
σ2=nRSS​.​
(67)
To find its bias, substitute the model and use the orthogonal fit directions 1 and x, obtaining
RSS=∑i​εi2​−nεˉ2−Sxx​(∑i​xi​εi​)2​.
(68)
The three expectations are nσ2, σ2, and σ2, respectively: Var(εˉ)=σ2/n and Var(∑i​xi​εi​)=σ2Sxx​. Hence ERSS=(n−2)σ2, giving the unbiased estimator
s2=n−2RSS​=n−2n​σ2.​
(69)
With n>2, a zero residual sum of squares is a probability-zero event in the model. For that exceptional dataset the likelihood is unbounded as σ2↓0, rather than having a maximum at a positive variance. In the intercept-only case Sxx​=0, the corresponding unbiased multiplier is n/(n−1) for n>1.

Set e=1/n​ and f=x/Sxx​​. These are orthonormal because ∑i​xi​=0. Complete them to an orthonormal basis e,f,q3​,…,qn​ of Rn. An orthogonal transformation of the standard normal error vector ε/σ has independent normal random variables as coordinates Z1​,…,Zn​: its joint probability density remains (2π)−n/2exp(−∥z∥2/2) because the transformation preserves squared length and has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one.
Projection onto these basis directions gives
α=α+n​σ​Z1​,β​=β+Sxx​​σ​Z2​,σ2RSS​=∑j=3n​Zj2​.
(70)
Therefore the joint distribution of least-squares and variance estimators is
α∼N(α,σ2/n),β​∼N(β,σ2/Sxx​),σ2nσ2​∼χn−22​,all three independent.​
(71)
The last law is the chi-squared distribution of a sum of n−2 squared independent normal random variables with mean zero and variance one, and independence follows because the three statistics use disjoint independent coordinate sets. When all xi​=0, omit the slope direction: α and nσ2/σ2∼χn−12​ are independent, and there is no identifiable slope estimator.

Under the null hypothesis, the standardized intercept Z=n​(α−α0​)/σ is standard normal, and V=RSS/σ2 is independent with chi-squared distribution of ν=n−2 degrees of freedom. Consequently the Student t test for a simple-regression intercept uses
T=s/n​α−α0​​=V/ν​Z​∼tn−2​under H0​.​
(72)
Choose a significance level γ∈(0,1) before observing the test result. For the two-sided alternative, reject H0​ when ∣T∣>tn−2,1−γ/2​, where the subscript denotes the indicated quantile of the Student t-distribution. The null rejection probability is exactly γ, independent of the nuisance slope and variance. Equivalently report the p-value 2[1−Ftn−2​​(∣Tobs​∣)]. The test assumes the normal independent-error model and a positive residual variance estimate. In the intercept-only case with n>1, use s2=RSS/(n−1) and tn−1​ instead.

Use payoff P=−(2x1​−3x2​−2x3​), so maximization of P is equivalent to the required minimization. In the given simplex tableau, x1​ can increase the payoff. The simplex ratio test has candidate ratios 3/6=1/2 in the z2​ row and 15/1=15 in the z3​ row; the negative coefficient in the x2​ row imposes no upper bound. Thus x1​ enters the simplex basis and z2​ leaves.
Divide the pivot row by 6, then eliminate x1​ from the other rows. The resulting simplex dictionary is
x1​−23​x3​−61​z1​+61​z2​x2​+21​x3​+31​z1​+61​z2​z3​+10x3​+613​z1​−61​z2​P+25​x3​+34​z1​+61​z2​​=21​,=3,=229​,=8.​

(x1​,x2​,x3​)=(21​,3,0),min(2x1​−3x2​−2x3​)=−8.​
